tips.title: BMI divides by height squared
tips.body: $\text{BMI} = \dfrac{\text{mass in kg}}{(\text{height in m})^2}$. Dividing by the height once instead of squaring it is the standard slip, and it makes every BMI far too large.

tips.title: Correlation is not cause
tips.body: Data showing smokers get more heart disease shows a **correlation**. Saying it **causes** it needs a mechanism as well. Write "is a risk factor for" unless the question gives you the biology.

tips.title: Risk factors interact
tips.body: Diet, exercise, alcohol and smoking are not independent. A question asking why one person is at more risk usually wants **two or more** factors and how they combine.

tips.title: Square the height before dividing
tips.body: On the calculator, work out **height × height first**, then divide the mass by it in one go. Typing mass ÷ height × height gives the wrong answer, because the calculator divides and then multiplies. One bracket, or one stored value, removes the risk entirely.

why.matters:
These diseases are not caught, so there is no route to cut and no vaccine to give. What there is instead is **risk**: things that make a disease more likely without making it certain, which is a much harder idea to reason about.

So this topic is partly biology and partly how to read evidence. A correlation is not a cause until there is a mechanism; a measurement like BMI is a rough guide and not a diagnosis; and *more likely* is not *will*.

examples.title: Why a risk factor is not a cause
examples.body:
Smokers get more heart disease than non-smokers. That is a **correlation** — the two things go together — and on its own it does not establish that one produces the other.

What turns it into a cause is a **mechanism**: something in the smoke damages the lining of the arteries, fatty deposits build up there, the vessel narrows. Now the link is explained rather than observed. The distinction matters because plenty of correlations have no mechanism at all, and a question asking whether data *proves* something is asking exactly this.

visual.alt: A table separating a correlation, which shows two things going together, from a mechanism, which shows how one produces the other, and notes that even both together give a risk rather than a certainty for any one person

examples.title: Why BMI puts a rugby player in the obese band
examples.body:
BMI is mass divided by height **squared**. A 105 kg forward who is 1.85 m tall works out at **30.7**, which the bands call obese — and so does a much less fit person of exactly the same height and mass.

BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, because it only ever sees two numbers. That is not a reason to ignore it: across a population it is quick, cheap and useful. It is a reason to treat one person's number as a **screening** result rather than a diagnosis. And do square the height: dividing by 1.85 once gives 57, which should look obviously wrong.

visual.alt: A table of the BMI bands: under eighteen point five is underweight, eighteen point five to twenty-four point nine is healthy, twenty-five to twenty-nine point nine is overweight and thirty or more is obese

examples.title: Why one habit turns up in several diseases
examples.body:
The same few risk factors keep appearing against different illnesses, which looks suspicious until you look at the mechanisms — they are genuinely different chains that happen to start in the same place.

Smoking damages arteries **and** the alveoli, so it raises the risk of both heart disease and lung disease by two separate routes. Obesity makes cells less responsive to insulin, which is type 2 diabetes, and also strains the heart. One behaviour, several mechanisms — which is why advice about lifestyle sounds repetitive and is not.

steps.title: Many causes, not one
steps.body:
A **non-communicable disease** cannot be caught. It usually has no single cause: it comes from the **interaction of a number of factors**.

- **Genes** you inherit.
- **Lifestyle**: diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol.
- **Environment**: air pollution, where you live and work.
- **Age**: the risk of most of these diseases rises with age.

Each one is a **risk factor**: something that makes a disease *more likely*, not certain. The specification names the main groups: **cardiovascular diseases**, many forms of **cancer**, some **lung** and **liver** diseases, and diseases influenced by **nutrition**.

steps.title: Diet, exercise, obesity and malnutrition
steps.body:
If you take in more **energy** from food than you use, the extra is stored as fat. Over time that leads to **obesity**, which raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and some cancers. **Exercise** uses energy and so helps keep the balance.

**Malnutrition** is not just *too little food*. It means a diet without the right balance: too little energy or too little of a nutrient (such as a vitamin or protein), or too much. In some places people cannot get enough food; in others they eat far more energy than they use. Both are forms of malnutrition.

visuals.alt: A table comparing obesity and undernutrition, their causes and effects

check.solution: **Malnutrition** is an unbalanced diet — too little *or* too much of something.

markScheme.description: a diet without the right balance

options: eating any amount of fatty food
being below a healthy weight only
not taking enough exercise
a diet without the right balance of nutrients

steps.title: Calculating BMI
steps.body:
**Body mass index** (BMI) compares mass with height:

**BMI = mass (kg) ÷ height (m)²**

Square the height first, then divide. The NHS uses these bands for adults: **below 18.5** underweight; **18.5 to 24.9** healthy weight; **25 to 29.9** overweight; **30 or more** obese.

BMI has a limit: it only uses mass and height, so it cannot tell **muscle from fat**.

visuals.problem: A person has a mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.80 m. Find their BMI.
Rearranging: what mass gives a BMI of 25 at 1.80 m?

check.prompt: A person has a mass of 81 kg and a height of 1.80 m. Calculate their BMI.

steps.title: Waist-to-hip ratio
steps.body:
The **waist-to-hip ratio** shows *where* fat is stored:

**waist-to-hip ratio = waist circumference ÷ hip circumference**

Measure both in the same units, so they cancel and the ratio has none. A higher ratio means more fat around the abdomen, and fat stored there is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. An exam question will give you any values to compare against.

visuals.problem: Waist 90 cm, hips 100 cm. Find the ratio.

check.prompt: Waist 76 cm, hips 95 cm. Calculate the waist-to-hip ratio.

steps.title: Alcohol and the liver
steps.body:
The **liver** breaks down alcohol, which is a **toxin**. Drinking too much over many years damages and kills liver cells.

- At first fat builds up in the liver.
- Damaged cells are replaced by **scar tissue**: this is **cirrhosis**, and a scarred liver cannot do its jobs properly.
- The risk of **liver cancer** rises.

Alcohol is a risk factor, not a certain cause: how much damage it does depends on how much and how long, and on other factors such as genes.

visuals.problem: How does heavy drinking lead to liver disease?

steps.text: The liver breaks down alcohol, a toxin

So the liver cannot work properly, and the risk of liver cancer rises

check.prompt: What name is given to scarring of the liver caused by long-term heavy drinking?
check.solution: **Cirrhosis**. Long-term alcohol use damages liver cells, and the scar tissue that replaces them cannot carry out the liver's functions, so the damage is permanent.

markScheme.description: cirrhosis

steps.title: Smoking and cardiovascular disease
steps.body:
**Cardiovascular disease** is disease of the heart and blood vessels. Smoking raises the risk in several ways.

- Chemicals in smoke **damage the lining of the arteries**. **Fatty deposits** build up at the damage and narrow the arteries.
- **Nicotine** raises heart rate and **blood pressure**, which damages the arteries further.
- **Carbon monoxide** reduces how much oxygen the blood can carry, so the heart has to work harder.

If the **coronary arteries**, which supply the heart muscle, narrow or are blocked by a clot, part of the heart muscle gets no oxygen: a **heart attack**. A clot that blocks an artery to the brain causes a **stroke**.

steps.title: Local, national and global
steps.body:
The specification asks for the effect of lifestyle factors at three **levels**. The trick is to say what changes at *that* level.

- **Local**: more people in an area needing GP and hospital care; families caring for relatives; people off work in local businesses.
- **National**: the cost to the health service of treating these diseases; fewer people able to work, so less tax is paid; less money for other services.
- **Global**: obesity rising across the world, including in lower- and middle-income countries, while malnutrition from too little food continues in the poorest places; smoking falling in some countries and still common in others.

No numbers here are needed: an exam question that wants them will give them to you.

rows: demand on GPs and hospitals; carers; lost work
health service costs; less tax; fewer workers

steps.title: Treating cardiovascular disease
steps.body:
There are three kinds of treatment, and the specification asks you to **evaluate** them.

**Life-long medication**
- **Statins** lower blood cholesterol, slowing the build-up of fatty deposits.
- **Anticoagulants**, such as warfarin, and antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin make clots less likely.
- **Antihypertensives** lower blood pressure.

**Surgical procedures**
- A **stent**, a mesh tube, holds a narrowed artery open.
- A **bypass** uses a blood vessel from elsewhere in the body to carry blood round a blockage.
- A **heart transplant** replaces a failing heart.

**Lifestyle changes**: stop smoking, eat less saturated fat and salt, exercise more, drink less alcohol.

visuals.alt: A table of the three types of treatment for cardiovascular disease with an advantage and a disadvantage of each

check.solution: A **stent** is a mesh tube that keeps the artery open so blood can flow.

steps.title: How to write an 'evaluate' answer
steps.body: An *evaluate* question on these treatments may be a longer, level-marked question. The top level needs **both sides of each treatment** and a **justified conclusion**. A plan helps.

visuals.problem: Evaluate the treatments for cardiovascular disease

steps.text: Medication: for — no operation; against — lifelong, side effects
steps.note: One for, one against, for each

steps.text: Surgery: for — quick, fixes a severe blockage; against — risks of infection and bleeding, recovery time
Lifestyle: for — cheap, no side effects, helps other diseases too; against — slow, depends on the person
Conclusion: it depends on severity — surgery for a severe blockage, lifestyle and medication for early risk; usually combined

steps.title: Going deeper: risk, levels and judgements
steps.body:
Three habits lift answers in this topic.

**Risk, not cause.** Write that smoking *increases the risk* of cardiovascular disease, and that non-communicable diseases come from *several factors interacting*. A study showing a link is evidence of a risk factor, not proof that everyone affected will get the disease.

**Say which level.** For local, national and global questions, name the level and give an effect that belongs to it — the health service budget is national, a busy GP surgery is local.

**Judge.** For treatments, weigh each one and conclude. The best conclusions depend on the patient: *for a severe blockage, surgery; for early risk, lifestyle and medication.*

And with BMI, know its limit: it cannot tell muscle from fat, which is why doctors also use the waist-to-hip ratio.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Non-communicable diseases** come from the **interaction of factors**: genes, lifestyle, environment, age. A **risk factor** raises the chance; it does not make a disease certain.
- **Diet and exercise**: energy in above energy used leads to **obesity**; **malnutrition** is any unbalanced diet, too little or too much.
- **BMI = mass (kg) ÷ height (m)²**. Adult bands: under 18.5, 18.5 to 24.9, 25 to 29.9, 30 or more. It cannot tell muscle from fat.
- **Waist-to-hip ratio = waist ÷ hip**: shows fat stored around the abdomen.
- **Alcohol** damages liver cells: **cirrhosis**, and a higher risk of liver cancer.
- **Smoking** damages artery linings, so fatty deposits narrow them; nicotine raises blood pressure; carbon monoxide cuts oxygen. Blocked coronary artery: heart attack.
- **Levels**: local, national, global — name the level and give an effect that belongs to it.
- **Treatments**: medication (statins, anticoagulants, for life), surgery (stents, bypass, transplant), lifestyle changes. Evaluate each and conclude.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of medication, surgery and lifestyle changes to treat cardiovascular disease.
questions.solution: For each treatment an advantage and a disadvantage, then a judgement. Medication: no operation, but taken for life, with side effects. Surgery: fast and effective for a severe blockage, but risks of infection, bleeding and anaesthetic, and a recovery time. Lifestyle: cheap, no side effects, improves health overall, but slow, needs willpower, and not enough alone for severe disease. Judgement: depends on how severe; often combined.

Surgery weighed: fast for severe blockages, but risks and recovery

questions.modelAnswer: **Medication** such as statins, which lower cholesterol, and anticoagulants, which reduce clotting, avoids an operation, but it has to be taken for life and can have side effects. **Surgery**, such as fitting a stent or a bypass, works quickly and can restore blood flow through a badly blocked artery, but every operation carries risks of infection, bleeding and reactions to the anaesthetic, and needs recovery time. **Lifestyle changes** — stopping smoking, eating less saturated fat, exercising more — are cheap and have no side effects, and they reduce the risk of other diseases too, but they take a long time to work and depend on the person keeping them up. The best choice depends on how severe the disease is: someone with a severe blockage needs surgery quickly, while someone at early risk may manage with lifestyle changes and medication. In practice they are usually combined, because lifestyle changes help every treatment work better.

questions.prompt: A scatter diagram plots the number of cigarettes each person in a sample smokes a day against their resting blood pressure. The points rise from the bottom left of the diagram to the top right. What does the diagram show?
questions.solution: **A positive correlation.** When the points on a scatter diagram rise from bottom left to top right, the two variables increase together: here, people who smoke more tend to have higher blood pressure. Points need not lie on a line for there to be a correlation; a correlation is a trend across the sample. Nor is a correlation proof of cause on its own. The biological reason here is that nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure, and it is this mechanism, together with the pattern in the data, that justifies calling smoking a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

questions.prompt: A study followed 10 000 adults for twenty years. Compared with non-smokers of healthy weight, the risk of coronary heart disease was 2.5 times greater for smokers of healthy weight, 2 times greater for obese non-smokers, and 6 times greater for people who were both smokers and obese. Which conclusion is best supported by these figures?
questions.solution: **The factors interact.** On their own, smoking multiplied the risk by 2.5 and obesity by 2. If the two simply added their extra risk, the combined figure would be about 3.5 times; even multiplying them gives 5. The observed figure, 6 times, is larger than either, which is what is meant by non-communicable diseases being caused by the **interaction of a number of factors**: each factor raises the risk, and together they raise it further still. The figures do not make the disease certain for anyone; a risk factor makes a disease more likely, not inevitable, and both smoking and obesity clearly carry a risk on their own.

markScheme.description: the two risk factors interact: together they raise the risk by more than the separate increases suggest

The two risk factors interact: together they raise the risk by more than the two separate increases would suggest
Everyone who both smokes and is obese will develop coronary heart disease within twenty years of the start of the study

questions.prompt: A 50-year-old patient has mildly narrowed coronary arteries and no chest pain. The patient smokes and takes little exercise. Which treatment is the most appropriate first step, and why?
questions.skill: choosing a treatment for mild disease
questions.solution: **Lifestyle changes first, perhaps with medication.** The narrowing is mild and causes no symptoms, so the aim is to stop it getting worse. Stopping smoking removes the chemicals that damage artery linings and the nicotine that raises blood pressure; more exercise and less saturated fat slow the build-up of fatty deposits; a statin lowers blood cholesterol. These carry little risk, though they depend on the patient keeping to them, and a statin is taken for life. Surgery has risks of its own: infection, bleeding and clots. A stent or bypass is justified when an artery is badly blocked, and a transplant only when the heart itself is failing. No treatment removes fatty deposits for good, and nothing makes a heart attack certain or impossible.

markScheme.description: lifestyle changes, possibly with a statin, because the narrowing is mild and these avoid the risks of surgery

options: Lifestyle changes, possibly with a statin, because the narrowing is mild and these lower the risk without the dangers of an operation
A stent fitted at once, because the mesh tube holds the artery open permanently and makes any change to the patient's habits unnecessary
Bypass surgery, because taking a blood vessel from elsewhere in the body is the only treatment that removes the fatty deposits for good
A heart transplant, because replacing the heart now avoids the heart attack that narrowed coronary arteries will otherwise certainly cause

questions.prompt: Name the measure of body size that is calculated by dividing a person's mass in kilograms by the square of their height in metres.
questions.solution: **Body mass index (BMI).** BMI = mass (kg) ÷ height (m)². Square the height first, then divide. For adults, a BMI below 18.5 is classed as underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 healthy weight, 25 to 29.9 overweight and 30 or more obese. BMI uses only mass and height, so it cannot tell muscle from fat, which is why a waist-to-hip ratio is often measured as well.

markScheme.description: body mass index (BMI)

questions.prompt: In one country, 6 400 people died from alcohol-related liver disease in 2010. In 2020 the figure was 8 000. Calculate the percentage increase in the number of deaths.
questions.solution: Increase $= 8\,000 - 6\,400 = 1\,600$. Percentage increase $= \dfrac{1\,600}{6\,400} \times 100 = 25\%$. A rise in deaths across a whole country is an effect at the **national** scale: more treatment for the health service to pay for, and more people lost to the workforce. Alcohol is a toxin that the liver breaks down; years of heavy drinking kill liver cells, which are replaced by scar tissue (cirrhosis), and raise the risk of liver cancer.

markScheme.description: finds the increase, 1 600, and divides it by the original 6 400 (× 100)

questions.prompt: A man's waist measures 90 cm and his hips 95 cm. Waist-to-hip ratio = waist ÷ hips. His doctor uses a ratio of 0.90 as the upper limit of the lower-risk range for men. Calculate by how many centimetres the man's waist would need to decrease, with his hip measurement unchanged, for his ratio to fall to 0.90.
questions.solution: His ratio now is $\dfrac{90}{95} = 0.947$, above the doctor's limit. For a ratio of 0.90 with hips of 95 cm, the waist must be $0.90 \times 95 = 85.5$ cm. Decrease needed $= 90 - 85.5 = 4.5$ cm. The waist-to-hip ratio shows **where** fat is stored: fat around the abdomen is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, which is why it is measured alongside BMI, which cannot tell muscle from fat.

markScheme.description: rearranges: waist = 0.90 × 95 = 85.5 cm
subtracts from the present waist: 90 − 85.5
4.5 cm

questions.prompt: Cigarette smoke contains nicotine and carbon monoxide. Explain how each of these increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, and describe what happens if a coronary artery becomes blocked.
questions.solution: **Nicotine** raises heart rate and **blood pressure**, which damages the artery walls, and fatty deposits build up at the damage and narrow the arteries. **Carbon monoxide** reduces the amount of **oxygen** the blood can carry, so the heart has to work harder to supply the body. If a **coronary artery**, which supplies the heart muscle, is blocked, part of the heart muscle receives no oxygen and cannot respire, and that is a **heart attack**.

carbon monoxide reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry, so the heart has to work harder
a blocked coronary artery starves part of the heart muscle of oxygen, causing a heart attack

Explains that carbon monoxide reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry, so the heart has to work harder
Describes that a blocked coronary artery leaves part of the heart muscle without oxygen, causing a heart attack

questions.modelAnswer: Nicotine raises the heart rate and the blood pressure. High blood pressure damages the lining of the arteries, and fatty deposits build up where the lining is damaged, narrowing the arteries and making a blockage more likely. Carbon monoxide binds to the red blood cells and reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry, so the heart has to beat harder and faster to deliver the oxygen the body needs, which puts further strain on it. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with blood. If one of them is narrowed by fatty deposits and then blocked, for example by a clot, the part of the heart muscle it supplies receives no oxygen and cannot respire, so it stops working: this is a heart attack.

questions.prompt: A student surveys 40 members of one gym and finds no link between BMI and cardiovascular disease. The student concludes that BMI has nothing to do with the risk of cardiovascular disease. Give three reasons why this conclusion is not reliable.
questions.skill: sampling and the limits of BMI
questions.solution: First, the **sample is small**: with 40 people, chance has a large effect and the result might not be repeated in another 40. Second, it is **not representative**: members of one gym are likely to be fitter, and more muscular, than the population as a whole, so a pattern in the whole population could be missing from this group. Third, **BMI cannot tell muscle from fat**: muscular gym members can have a high BMI without the body fat that raises the risk, so BMI is a poor measure of fat in exactly this group. Cardiovascular disease also develops over decades, so a single survey of mostly healthy people would not show the risk anyway. A study showing no link in this sample does not overturn the evidence from large, representative studies that obesity is a risk factor.

the sample is not representative: members of one gym are likely to be fitter and more muscular than the population as a whole

BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so muscular gym members with a high BMI do not carry the body fat that raises risk (or: the disease develops over decades, so one survey cannot show the risk; or: other risk factors such as age, smoking and genes were not controlled)

criteria.text: Says that the sample is small, so chance has a large effect and the result may not be repeatable
Says that the sample is not representative: members of one gym are likely to be fitter and more muscular than the population as a whole

Explains that BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so muscular gym members with a high BMI do not carry the body fat that raises risk, or that the disease develops over decades so a single survey cannot show the risk, or that other risk factors such as age, smoking and genes were not controlled and could hide a link

questions.modelAnswer: The sample is far too small. With only 40 people, a few individuals can change the result completely, so a pattern that exists in the population could easily be hidden by chance, and a second group of 40 might give a different answer. The sample is also not representative of the population. Everyone in it uses the same gym, so they are likely to be fitter, more active and more muscular than people in general, and a conclusion drawn from them cannot be applied to everyone. The choice of group matters especially for BMI, because BMI only uses mass and height and cannot tell muscle from fat. Muscular gym members can have a BMI in the overweight range while carrying little body fat, so in this group a high BMI does not mean the stored fat that raises the risk of cardiovascular disease, and the measure is at its least useful. Finally, cardiovascular disease develops over many years, so a single survey of mostly healthy adults would not be expected to show the risk even if it were there. Large, representative studies do show that obesity raises the risk, and one small survey of one gym does not overturn them.

questions.prompt: A 55-year-old man smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has a BMI of 31 and a waist-to-hip ratio of 1.02. For adults, a BMI of 30 or more is classed as obese, and in men a waist-to-hip ratio above 0.90 indicates fat stored around the abdomen. His doctor tells him that his risk of cardiovascular disease is far higher than any one of these figures suggests on its own. Explain how each of the three factors raises his risk, and explain why the doctor is right about their combined effect.
questions.solution: **Smoking**: chemicals in smoke damage the lining of the arteries, and **fatty deposits** build up at the damage and narrow them, including the **coronary arteries**; **nicotine** raises heart rate and blood pressure, and **carbon monoxide** reduces the oxygen the blood can carry, so the heart works harder. **BMI 31** is in the **obese** range, and obesity raises the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. The **ratio of 1.02** is above 0.90, so fat is stored around the **abdomen**, which is linked to a higher risk; it adds what BMI cannot show, since BMI uses only mass and height and says nothing about where fat is stored. Obesity itself raises **blood pressure** and **blood cholesterol**, which speeds the build-up of fatty deposits. If a narrowed coronary artery is blocked, part of the heart muscle gets no oxygen: a **heart attack**. Non-communicable diseases arise from the **interaction of a number of factors**, so the three risks combine to give a greater risk than any one alone, though it remains a risk, not a certainty, and lifestyle changes would lower it.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that smoking or obesity raises the risk of cardiovascular disease, or reads the BMI as obese, with little explanation of how

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains how two of the factors raise the risk, for example smoke damaging artery linings so fatty deposits narrow the arteries, and abdominal fat shown by the ratio, but does not explain the interaction or confuses the two measures

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): explains all three: smoke chemicals damage artery linings and fatty deposits narrow the coronary arteries, nicotine raises blood pressure and carbon monoxide cuts the oxygen carried; a BMI of 31 means obesity, which raises blood pressure and cholesterol; the ratio shows fat around the abdomen, linked to cardiovascular disease and not revealed by BMI; and concludes that the factors interact so the combined risk exceeds the separate ones, while still being a risk rather than a certainty

criteria.text: Explains that chemicals in smoke damage the lining of the arteries, so fatty deposits build up at the damage and narrow the arteries, including the coronary arteries
Explains that nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure, damaging the arteries further, and that carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen the blood can carry so the heart works harder
States that a BMI of 31 is in the obese range, and that obesity raises the risk of cardiovascular disease (and of type 2 diabetes)

Explains that a ratio of 1.02 is above 0.90, showing fat stored around the abdomen, which is linked to a higher risk and which BMI alone cannot show, because BMI uses only mass and height and says nothing about where fat is stored

Explains how obesity raises the risk: more energy taken in than used has been stored as fat, and obesity raises blood pressure and blood cholesterol, which speeds the build-up of fatty deposits in the arteries

Explains that non-communicable diseases come from the interaction of a number of factors, so the three risks combine to give a greater risk than any one alone, while remaining a risk rather than a certainty, and that lifestyle changes would lower it

questions.modelAnswer:
**Smoking.** Chemicals in cigarette smoke damage the lining of the arteries. **Fatty deposits** build up where the lining is damaged, and the arteries narrow, including the **coronary arteries** that supply the heart muscle. **Nicotine** raises the heart rate and the blood pressure, which damages the artery walls further, and **carbon monoxide** reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry, so the heart has to work harder for the same supply. Twenty cigarettes a day means this damage is happening continuously.

**BMI.** BMI is mass divided by height squared, and 31 is above 30, so he is in the **obese** range. Energy taken in beyond what he uses has been stored as fat. Obesity raises **blood pressure** and the level of **cholesterol** in the blood, both of which speed the build-up of fatty deposits in the arteries, so it raises the risk of cardiovascular disease, as well as of type 2 diabetes, itself a risk factor for heart disease.

**Waist-to-hip ratio.** A ratio of 1.02 is well above 0.90, so his waist is wider than his hips and the fat is stored around the **abdomen**. Fat stored there is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease than fat stored elsewhere. The ratio tells the doctor something BMI cannot: BMI uses only mass and height, so it cannot say where the fat is stored. Here the two measures agree.

**What is at stake.** Narrowed coronary arteries can be blocked completely by a clot. The heart muscle beyond the blockage receives no oxygen, cannot respire and stops working: a **heart attack**.

**Why the doctor is right.** Non-communicable diseases are caused by the **interaction of a number of factors**. Each of these three raises the risk on its own, and together they act on the same arteries at once: smoking damages the lining, while the fat and the strain on the heart make the deposits build up faster. The combined risk is therefore greater than any single figure suggests. It is still a **risk, not a certainty**: these factors make a heart attack more likely, not inevitable, and because they are lifestyle factors they can be changed. Stopping smoking, eating less saturated fat and taking more exercise would lower all three risks at once, which is why the doctor raises them together.

examTechnique.body:
Expect a calculation, an explanation and an evaluation from this topic. The calculations are BMI and the waist-to-hip ratio: square the height before dividing, rearrange confidently when the question gives the BMI and asks for mass, and remember that a ratio has no units. The explanations are chains — smoking to damaged arteries to narrowing to heart attack; alcohol to liver cell damage to cirrhosis.

The specification asks you to evaluate the treatments for cardiovascular disease (5.25), and that may be a longer, level-marked question. Give an advantage and a disadvantage for each of medication, surgery and lifestyle change, then a conclusion that depends on the patient. Throughout, use the language of risk: lifestyle factors increase the risk of a disease; they do not cause it in everyone.
examinerErrors: Dividing by the height instead of the height squared when calculating BMI.
Saying smoking will give a person heart disease: it increases the risk; not every smoker gets it.
Describing the three treatments without weighing them or reaching a conclusion.
Giving a local effect when the question asks for national or global.
Saying a stent lowers cholesterol, or a statin opens the artery: the two are often swapped.
Treating malnutrition as meaning only too little food.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer calculates BMI and the waist-to-hip ratio cleanly, including rearranging BMI to find a mass, and knows that BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. It explains how smoking and alcohol lead to disease as causal chains, uses the language of risk factors and interacting causes, and places each effect at the right level. On treatments it weighs medication, surgery and lifestyle change and reaches a conclusion that depends on how severe the disease is.
